thread.title: WeWork: Saudi Arabia And Abu Dhabi Are Right - WeWork (Private:VWORK)

author: Crispus Nyaga
title: WeWork: Saudi Arabia And Abu Dhabi Are Right - WeWork (Private:VWORK)
text:
Source: FT
Thesis
On Wednesday, Wall Street Journal reported that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund ( PIF ) and Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investments had cautioned Softbank ( OTCPK:SFTBF ) against increasing its ownership of WeWork ( VWORK ). The article said :
PIF and Mubadala have questioned the wisdom of doubling down on WeWork, and have cast doubt on its rich valuation. The company is on track to lose around $2 billion this year, and the funds have expressed concern that WeWork’s model could leave it exposed if the economy turns down.
The two countries, which have contributed the bulk of the Vision Fund are right to question the current deal which values WeWork at more than $45 billion. This article will explain why the two countries are right with their thinking.
Vision Fund
Source: Bloomberg
Masayoshi Son is the richest man in Japan. At a point during the dot com bubble, he was the richest man on earth but saw his net worth decrease by more than 99%. Since then, he has transformed Softbank from a small telecom company in Japan to become one of the most influential technology company in the world. In 2016, Son launched the Vision Fund to offer investments to technology companies. To date, the fund has made large investments in companies like WeWork, Uber ( UBER ), Nvidia ( NVDA ), and ByteDance among others. A summary of some of the investments are summarized below.
Source: Yahoo Finance
The Contentious Deal
SoftBank has invested billions of dollars to become one of the biggest shareholders in WeWork. In 2017, the company invested more than $4.4 billion in the company. The investment valued WeWork at more than $20 billion. In November this year, SoftBank committed $4 billion to the company in a deal that valued it at more than $45 billion. The current deal being negotiated will see SoftBank add between $16 billion and $20 billion to the company.
WeWork
WeWork operates a very simple business model. The company negotiates long-term leases with developers, revamps the offices, and then makes short-term leases with entrepreneurs, startups, and established companies like Citi (NYSE: C ), Facebook ( FB ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ) among others. According to its website, it has 517 locations in more than 96 cities around the world. It has more than 270,000 members who pay about $500 for a desk for month. The company tapped into an industry that is growing and one that is addressing the costs of office ownership among startups. A report by IWG showed that the industry is growing as shown below.
Source: IWG
Is WeWork Worth $45 Billion?
The leaders of PIC and Mubadala are right to question the valuation that SoftBank is paying for WeWork. This is especially after the recent happenings in the stock market where once-flying startups like Blue Apron ( APRN ), Snap ( SNAP ) and GoPro ( GPRO ) have become shadows of former selves after debuting in the public market.
Like Uber did not invent the field of ride sharing, WeWork did not invent the field of office sharing. For more than 30-years, IWG ( OTC:IWGFF ) – formerly known as Regus - has been providing the same services. To date, the company helps more than 2.5 million people and companies every year work in a shared environment. It is available in more than 3300 cities in more than 110 countries. It offers these services using a number of brands as shown below:
Source: IWG
While the two companies are in different phases of growth, it is easy to compare the valuation of WeWork with that of IWG because of the similarity of their businesses. IWG is listed at the London Stocks Exchange ( LSE ) and is a member of the FTSE 100 companies. The company is currently valued at more than £1.8 billion, with investors paying ~16X last 12 months earnings. It also has a dividend yield of 2.89%.
As a private company, WeWork does not release its quarterly earnings and the management is not obligated to issuing conference calls. However, in August, the company released its Q2 performance that showed impressive growth. In the quarter, the company’s revenues rose to more than $421 million from $198 million a year ago. However, its losses jumped to $723 million in the first half of the year from $154 million in the previous year. This loss was expected as the company is continuing expanding its physical presence. Its operating margins – excluding expenses – rose to 28% while the occupancy rate increased to 84%. The company is expected to lose more than $2 billion this year.
Therefore, while WeWork has shown a lot of progress in growth, it is difficult to justify the valuation SoftBank wants to pay. In a July article by Financial Times , Elaine Moore and Erin Platt valued the company at just $3 billion. This valuation was before SoftBank announced the new cash injection. This valuation applied the same multiple as IWG. However, I believe that comparing IWG and WeWork from a multiple standpoint is wrong for two reasons.
First, IWG is an already mature company that is seeing some weaker growth. It is like valuing a fast-growing fintech company like Square ( SQ ) and an old fintech company like Visa ( V ). Second, WeWork is benefiting from the hype surrounding startups.
Still, the $45 billion SoftBank is offering values it at ~20X estimated 2018 revenue which is pricey. Forbes estimates that WeWork could double its revenue by 2022. Even if it does, its $45 billion valuation would not make sense currently. This is because even with a $4 billion annual revenue, and a net profit margin of 6% similar to IWG, its net income for the year will be $240 million. Therefore, the valuation will be ~ 187X net income. The company’s lower margin will be warranted because it is not a technology company but an office space rental company.
Saudis and Abu Dhabi fund managers are also right to worry about the Vision Fund’s exposure to one company. If the deal Son is negotiating goes through, the fund will be the majority owner while WeWork’s founder, Adam Neumann will be the controlling shareholder. The $16 billion investment will represent more than 10% of the total amount of the Vision Fund. Therefore, they are worried about the risks that could happen especially if the management fails to execute to perfection. This is more worrisome at a time when interest rates are going up, markets are becoming volatile, and the risks of a recession are rising by the day.
Key Takeaways
Masayoshi Son is an incredible investor who has made billions of dollars for his investors. However, like other investors, he is not perfect as evidenced by his decisions during the dot com bubble. As the biggest investors in the Vision Fund, Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi are right to point out the risks of the WeWork deal. This is mostly because of the fact that the current valuation simply does not make sense and the fact that Son is valuing it as a technology company of which its not.
